concepts.title: Sampling
concepts.one_liner: Sampling is the process of transforming a continuous signal into a discrete one to enable computer processing.
concepts.content: In nature, most signals we measure, such as sound and light, are defined over continuous domains like time and space. In order to process these signals with computers, the continuous domain must be transformed into a discrete one. Sampling is the specific process of transforming a continuous signal into a discrete one.
concepts.motivation_md: Since digital computers cannot process continuous data directly, sampling is required to convert real-world signals into a format that can be stored and manipulated digitally.
concepts.recap_md: - Sampling converts continuous signals (like sound or light) into discrete data.

concepts.title: Sampling Period
concepts.one_liner: The sampling period $T_s$ is the time interval between successive samples in the conversion of a continuous signal to a discrete one.
concepts.content: Consider a one-dimensional (1D) continuous time signal $\ell (t)$ and its sampled version $\ell [n] = \ell(n T_s)$, where $T_s$ is the sampling period. In this sampling process, some information is inevitably lost. To recover the continuous signal $\ell (t)$ from its sampled version $\ell [n]$ through interpolation, one must ensure information loss is minimized. Decreasing $T_s$ results in a more accurate approximation of the continuous signal $\ell (t)$, but increases the memory needed to store $\ell [n]$ and the computational cost of processing. Therefore, choosing the appropriate $T_s$ is necessary to find optimal sampling parameters and allow for signal reconstruction.
concepts.motivation_md: The sampling period determines the balance between signal fidelity and resource consumption (memory and CPU), making its selection critical for efficient digital signal processing.
concepts.recap_md: - The sampling period $T_s$ defines the interval at which a continuous signal is measured.

concepts.title: Aliasing
concepts.one_liner: Aliasing is the confusion of frequencies that occurs when a signal is sampled improperly.
concepts.content: When parameters for sampling are chosen such that different frequencies become indistinguishable, a specific qualitative behavior occurs. This confusion of frequencies is called aliasing.
concepts.motivation_md: Aliasing represents a fundamental limit in sampling; understanding it is crucial to avoid distortions where high-frequency signals masquerade as lower-frequency ones.
concepts.recap_md: - Aliasing is the phenomenon where different signal frequencies become indistinguishable due to sampling.

concepts.one_liner: A band-limited signal is a signal with no spectral content above a specific maximum frequency $w_{max}$.

concepts.motivation_md: The concept of band-limiting is central to the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem, as it defines the conditions under which a continuous signal can be perfectly reconstructed from its samples.

concepts.title: Linear interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Linear interpolation consists of interpolating linearly between two consecutive values using a triangular kernel.
concepts.content:
In 1D, popular interpolation kernels include nearest interpolation and linear interpolation. Nearest interpolation consists of assigning to each time instant the value of the nearest sample in time. Linear interpolation consists of interpolating linearly between two consecutive values.

Both methods can be modeled as a linear convolution with a kernel $h(t)$:

(see figure: (top) Nearest interpolation. (bottom) Linear interpolation. Both interpolation methods can be modeled by a convolution with the kernel shown in the middle (a box and a triangle).)

The nearest neighbor interpolation is the result of the convolution of $\ell_\delta (t)$ with a box of width $T_s$. In linear interpolation, the interpolation kernel $h(t)$ is a triangle of width $2T_s$.
concepts.motivation_md: Interpolation is necessary to reconstruct a continuous signal from discrete samples. Linear interpolation provides a simple way to estimate values between samples by assuming a straight-line relationship, which is more accurate than nearest-neighbor assignment.
concepts.recap_md: - Linear interpolation estimates values by connecting consecutive samples with straight lines.

concepts.title: Lanczos-1 interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Lanczos-1 interpolation uses the central lobe of the sinc function as a kernel to provide smooth local interpolation.
concepts.content: Lanczos-1 interpolation consists of using as a kernel only the central lobe of the sinc function. This provides an interpolation that is smooth while using only a local neighborhood. Other interpolation methods, such as cubic interpolation, can also be written as convolutions. Note that the convolution of two box filters of width $T_s/2$ results in a triangle of length $T_s$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard linear interpolation can be too blocky or sharp. Lanczos-1 uses a windowed sinc function to provide a smoother reconstruction of the signal while keeping the computation efficient by only looking at a local neighborhood of samples.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses the central lobe of the sinc function as the interpolation kernel.

concepts.title: Rectangular sampling
concepts.one_liner: Rectangular sampling is a 2D sampling pattern where a continuous image is sampled on a regular grid.
concepts.content:
When sampling 2D signals to form discrete images, a continuous image $\ell (x,y)$ can be sampled using a rectangular grid as $\ell_s [n,m] = \ell (nT_x, mT_y)$. This is a specific case of a more general sampling pattern defined as:

$$\ell_s [n,m] = \ell (an+bm, cn+dm)$$

where $a,b,c,d$ are constants. If $a=T, b=0, c=0, d=T$, the result is regular rectangular sampling. Other patterns, such as hexagonal or irregular sampling, are also possible.

(see figure: Three types of sampling: rectangular grid, hexagonal, and irregular.)
concepts.motivation_md: Rectangular sampling is the standard method for digital imaging because it aligns perfectly with the matrix-based representation of images in computer memory and displays.
concepts.recap_md: - Samples a continuous 2D signal on a regular grid defined by fixed intervals $T_x$ and $T_y$.

key_passage.text: If we have a continuous image ℓ (x,y) we can sample it using a rectangular grid as ℓs [n,m] = ℓ (nTx, mTy). We can do a very similar analysis to the one we just did for the 1D case. But in 2D, we can have more interesting sampling patterns.

concepts.title: Hexagonal sampling
concepts.one_liner: Hexagonal sampling is a 2D sampling pattern that can be defined by specific linear combinations of sample indices.
concepts.content:
In 2D signal sampling, we can define a discrete image using the general form:

$$\ell_s [n,m] = \ell (an+bm, cn+dm)$$

where $a,b,c,d$ are constants. If we set $a=T_1, b=-T_2 / 2, c=0, d=T_2$, we obtain hexagonal sampling. This is one of several possible patterns for arranging samples in a 2D space.

(see figure: Three types of sampling: rectangular grid, hexagonal, and irregular.)
concepts.motivation_md: Hexagonal sampling is more efficient than rectangular sampling, providing better radial symmetry and requiring fewer samples to represent the same amount of high-frequency information.

concepts.title: Irregular sampling
concepts.one_liner: Irregular sampling involves placing signal samples at random locations rather than on a fixed grid.
concepts.content:
Beyond regular patterns like rectangular or hexagonal grids, 2D signals can be sampled by placing the samples at random locations, known as irregular sampling. This contrasts with grid-based sampling where sample positions are determined by linear combinations of indices $n$ and $m$.

(see figure: Three types of sampling: rectangular grid, hexagonal, and irregular.)
concepts.motivation_md: Irregular sampling can help reduce aliasing artifacts that appear as structured patterns (like Moire patterns) by turning them into less distracting random noise.
concepts.recap_md: - Samples are placed at random or non-grid locations in the 2D plane.

concepts.title: Fourier transform of 2D sampled signals
concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of a 2D sampled signal is a sum of shifted replicas of the continuous signal's spectrum.
concepts.content:
To study aliasing in 2D, we model sampling by multiplying a continuous image $\ell(x,y)$ by a 2D delta train:

$$\ell_{\delta} (x,y) = \ell (x,y) \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta (x- an-bm, y - cn-dm)$$

Using vector notation where $\mathbf{x} = (x,y)^T$, $\mathbf{n} = (n,m)^T$, and $\mathbf{A}$ is the sampling matrix, the delta train is $\delta_{\mathbf{A}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{\mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{Z}^2} \delta ( \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{A} \mathbf{n} )$. The continuous Fourier transform of this sampled signal is:

$$\mathscr{L}_{\delta} (\mathbf{w}) =  \frac{(2 \pi)^2}{|\mathbf{A}|} \sum_{\mathbf{k} \in \mathbb{Z}^2} \mathscr{L} ( \mathbf{w} - 2 \pi \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{k} )$$

For a $2\times2$ matrix, the inverse is $\mathbf{A}^{-1} = \frac{1}{|\mathbf{A}|} \left[ \begin{array}{cc} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{array} \right]$. In the case of rectangular sampling, this simplifies to:

$$\mathscr{L}_{\delta} (w_x, w_y ) =  \frac{(2 \pi)^2}{T^2} \sum_{k_1=-\infty}^{\infty} \sum_{k_2=-\infty}^{\infty} \mathscr{L} (w_x - \frac{2\pi}{T}k_1, w_y - \frac{2\pi}{T}k_2 )$$
concepts.motivation_md: Analyzing the Fourier transform of sampled signals allows us to understand how the sampling pattern affects the spectral content and to determine the conditions necessary to avoid aliasing in 2D.
concepts.recap_md: - Sampling in the spatial domain results in periodic replication of the spectrum in the frequency domain.

concepts.title: Optimal 2D sampling arrangement
concepts.one_liner: Regular hexagonal sampling is the optimal 2D strategy, maximizing resolution for a fixed number of samples.
concepts.content:
The optimal sampling arrangement is the one that allows the best reconstruction of a continuous signal from a fixed number of samples by maximizing the region of valid frequencies without aliasing.

(see figure: Sketch of the Fourier transforms of the rectangular and hexagonal samplings. The red boundary denotes the spectral content that gets periodically repeated.)

Regular hexagonal sampling is the optimal strategy. While computer vision typically uses rectangular grids, hexagonal sampling achieves approximately a 10 percent increase in resolution for the same number of samples. This pattern is found in nature; for example, the distribution of photoreceptors in the primate fovea closely resembles a hexagonal array.

(see figure: Distributions of cones in the fovea of a Monkey \cite{Curcio1990)]

Hexagonal grids also allow for more efficient convolutional filters and better radial symmetry.
concepts.motivation_md: Finding the optimal sampling pattern is crucial for maximizing information capture and minimizing aliasing when resources (like the number of pixels or sensors) are limited.
concepts.recap_md: - Hexagonal sampling is more efficient than rectangular sampling, offering higher resolution for the same sample count.

concepts.title: Sampling finite size images
concepts.one_liner: Sampling results for infinite signals can be applied to finite images by extending them with zero padding.
concepts.content: While standard sampling analysis assumes signals of infinite length, real-world images have a finite size. The theoretical results derived for infinite signals can be applied to finite images by extending the image to infinity using zero padding.
concepts.motivation_md: Mathematical models of sampling often assume infinite domains for simplicity, but practical applications require a way to bridge this theory with finite, real-world data.
concepts.recap_md: - Finite images are treated as infinite signals via zero padding to apply standard sampling theory.

key_passage.text: The same results can be applied by extending the image to infinity with zero padding.

concepts.title: Aliasing in 2D images
concepts.one_liner: Sampling a 2D image at an insufficient frequency causes high-frequency details to appear as low-frequency artifacts, such as stripes changing orientation.
concepts.content:
Sampling with the wrong frequency has interesting effects in 2D. For example, a picture downsampled at different resolutions (412×512, 103×128, 52×64, and 26×32) and then reconstructed to the original resolution shows the effects of aliasing. The stripes on a zebra's body may change orientation as we downsample them, and at the lowest resolutions, the animal may become difficult to recognize. 

When we multiply the image with a delta train (one every four samples along each dimension), the image Fourier transform changes. The magnitude of the DFT of the sampled image changes substantially from one resolution to the next due to aliasing. (see figure: Subsampling with aliasing. (a) The zebra sampled with aliasing starts looking like a cow. (b) Fourier transform of the continuous signal $\ell(x,y)$ multiplied by delta trains: $\ell_{\delta}(x,y)$. (c) Discrete Fourier transform of the corresponding sampled signals, $\ell\left[n,m\right)$. (d) Fourier transform of the reconstructed signal with aliasing. (e) Sampled image after processing it with an anti-aliasing filter. (f) Discrete Fourier transform of the corresponding anti-aliased sampled images, $\ell\left[n,m\right]$. Note that now the central part of the Fourier transform is not changing.]
concepts.motivation_md: Aliasing in 2D images occurs when the sampling rate is too low to capture high-frequency spatial details, leading to visual distortions like Moire patterns or incorrect textures. Understanding this helps in designing better image sensors and reconstruction algorithms.

concepts.title: Anti-aliasing filter
concepts.one_liner: An anti-aliasing filter is a low-pass filter applied before sampling to make a signal band-limited and prevent high-frequency interference.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Subsampling with aliasing. (a) The zebra sampled with aliasing starts looking like a cow. (b) Fourier transform of the continuous signal $\ell(x,y)$ multiplied by delta trains: $\ell_{\delta}(x,y)$. (c) Discrete Fourier transform of the corresponding sampled signals, $\ell\left[n,m\right)$. (d) Fourier transform of the reconstructed signal with aliasing. (e) Sampled image after processing it with an anti-aliasing filter. (f) Discrete Fourier transform of the corresponding anti-aliased sampled images, $\ell\left[n,m\right]$. Note that now the central part of the Fourier transform is not changing.]

In order to reduce aliasing artifacts, we need to filter the continuous signal with a low-pass filter to make it band-limited. This allows us to sample the signal while avoiding high-spatial frequencies that interfere with the low-frequency content of the image. While the anti-aliasing filter does not prevent the loss of information contained in high spatial frequencies, it prevents that information from corrupting lower frequencies. Each resolution requires a different filter. The anti-aliasing filter can be a box filter with support equal to the appropriate region in the Fourier domain.
concepts.motivation_md: To prevent high-frequency noise and details from 'folding' into lower frequencies during sampling, which creates permanent distortions that cannot be removed later.

In order to reduce aliasing artifacts, we need to filter the continuous signal with a low-pass filter to make it band-limited. This allows us to sample the signal while avoiding high-spatial frequencies that interfere with the low-frequency content of the image. While the anti-aliasing filter does not prevent the loss of information contained in high spatial frequencies, it prevents that information from corrupting lower frequencies. Each resolution requires a different filter. The anti-aliasing filter can be a box filter with support equal to the appropriate region in the Fourier domain.

concepts.title: Spatiotemporal Sampling
concepts.one_liner: Spatiotemporal sampling extends sampling theory to $N$ dimensions, accounting for both spatial grids and temporal intervals.
concepts.content: Spatiotemporal sampling can be studied using general sampling equations in $N$ dimensions. Temporal aliasing is responsible for the typical illusion in which we see wheels or fans changing their sense of rotation in movies. To avoid those artifacts, it is important to apply an anti-aliasing filter to the signal before sampling.
concepts.motivation_md: Capturing moving images requires sampling in both space and time. Understanding this allows engineers to prevent temporal artifacts like the 'wagon-wheel effect'.

concepts.title: Global Shutter Mode
concepts.one_liner: Global shutter mode is a regular sampling method where all pixels in a 2D grid are exposed simultaneously at regular time intervals.
concepts.content: The most common type of spatiotemporal sampling is regular sampling. In this mode, all the pixels are sampled in a regular spatial 2D grid and at regular time instants in which all the pixels are exposed simultaneously. This is also called global shutter mode.
concepts.motivation_md: Global shuttering ensures that the entire frame represents a single point in time, preventing geometric distortion in images of fast-moving objects.
concepts.recap_md: ["- All pixels are exposed at the exact same instant.", "- Uses a regular spatial 2D grid and regular time intervals.", "- Avoids the spatial distortions common in rolling shutter systems."]

concepts.title: Rolling Shutter Mode
concepts.one_liner: Rolling shutter mode samples image rows at different time instants, allowing for faster sampling rates but potentially causing spatial distortions.
concepts.content: In many cameras, such as DSLRs and mobile phones, the most commonly used sampling is the rolling shutter mode. In this mode, every row in the image is sampled simultaneously, but different rows are sampled at different instants. This sampling mode allows for a faster sampling rate with current hardware implementations, but it can create spatial distortions in the image if the camera moves or when taking pictures of moving objects.
concepts.motivation_md: Rolling shutters are easier and cheaper to implement in CMOS sensors, allowing for high-resolution capture even if it introduces 'jello' effects or skewing during motion.
concepts.recap_md: ["- Rows of pixels are sampled sequentially rather than all at once.", "- Enables faster sampling rates in consumer hardware.", "- Can cause spatial distortions (skewing) when the camera or subject moves."]

concepts.title: Moire Patterns
concepts.one_liner: Moire patterns are interference patterns that appear when superposing semitransparent patterns on top of each other.
concepts.content:
Moire patterns, also related to aliasing, are interference patterns that appear when superposing semitransparent patterns on top of each other.

concepts.motivation_md: Moire patterns are a physical manifestation of aliasing that occurs when two repetitive structures overlap, creating a new, lower-frequency pattern.

concepts.title: Aliasing and Superresolution
concepts.one_liner: While often an artifact, aliasing can be used by superresolution algorithms to recover high-frequency details that would otherwise be lost.
concepts.content: Aliasing is a common artifact that appears whenever an image is captured by sampling a continuous light field, and it also affects images during upsampling or downsampling. However, aliasing is not always bad; it may be possible to use aliasing to recover high-frequency content that would be otherwise lost. Superresolution algorithms can learn to extract fine image details from the aliasing pattern. Additionally, when an image is encoded by multiple channels, aliasing in one channel does not mean information is lost, as multiple channels may contain complementary information allowing the recovery of high-resolution details.
concepts.motivation_md: To shift the perspective of aliasing from a purely destructive artifact to a potential source of hidden information that can be exploited to enhance image quality.
concepts.recap_md: ["- Aliasing occurs during sampling of continuous light fields or during rescaling.", "- Superresolution algorithms can exploit aliasing patterns to reconstruct fine details.", "- Multiple channels can provide complementary information to overcome aliasing in a single channel."]

concepts.title: Sampling Theorem (Nyquist Theorem)
concepts.one_liner: The sampling theorem states that a signal can be perfectly reconstructed if the sampling frequency is more than twice the maximum frequency present in the input signal.
concepts.content: The sampling theorem (also known as Nyquist theorem) states that for a signal to be perfectly reconstructed from a set of samples (under the slow and smooth prior), the sampling frequency $w_s = 2 \pi /T_s$ has to be $w_s > 2w_{max}$ when $w_{max}$ is the maximum frequency present in the input signal. The same theorem can be stated in terms of periods: the sampling period, $T_s$, has to be $T_s < T_{min} / 2$, which is smaller than half of the period of the highest frequency component, $T_{min} = 2 \pi /w_{max}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The sampling theorem provides the essential criterion for determining the minimum sampling rate required to capture all information in a continuous signal without loss.
concepts.recap_md: - The sampling frequency must be greater than twice the maximum frequency of the signal ($w_s > 2w_{max}$).- The sampling period must be less than half the period of the highest frequency component ($T_s < T_{min} / 2$).

concepts.title: Radian frequency
concepts.one_liner: Radian frequency $w$ is defined as $2\pi$ times the hertz frequency $f$.
concepts.content: In this book, we use the radian frequency for continuous signals, $w = 2 \pi f$, where $f$ is the hertz frequency. For a sinusoidal wave of period $T$ seconds, its frequency is $w=2\pi / T$.
concepts.motivation_md: Radian frequency is the standard unit for frequency in signal processing because it simplifies the mathematical representation of periodic functions by absorbing the $2\pi$ factor.
concepts.recap_md: - Radian frequency $w$ is related to hertz frequency $f$ by the formula $w = 2\pi f$.- For a signal with period $T$, the radian frequency is $w = 2\pi / T$.

concepts.title: Delta train (Impulse train, Dirac comb)
concepts.one_liner: The delta train is a periodic signal consisting of a sequence of Dirac delta impulses centered at regular time intervals.
concepts.content: The delta train distribution (also known as the impulse train or Dirac comb), $\delta_{T_s}(t)$, is a periodic signal with period $T_s$ composed of delta impulses centered at times $nT_s$. It is defined as: $$ \delta_{T_s}(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t-n T_s) $$ When $T_s = 1$, the delta train has the following shape: (see figure: Delta train with period $T_s=1$. The arrows show when the train's value is infinite. The height of each impulse represents its area.)
concepts.motivation_md: The delta train provides a rigorous mathematical way to represent the transition from a continuous-time signal to a discrete-time sequence of samples.
concepts.recap_md: - A delta train is a periodic sequence of Dirac delta impulses spaced by the sampling period $T_s$.- It is also known as an impulse train or a Dirac comb.

concepts.title: Modeling the Sampling Process
concepts.one_liner: The sampling process is modeled by multiplying a continuous signal with a delta train, resulting in a sequence of weighted impulses.
concepts.content: The delta train can be used to model the sampling process. Using the sampling property of the delta distribution $\ell (t) \delta (t-a) = \ell(a)$, multiplying a function $\ell(t)$ by the delta train $\delta_{T_s}(t)$ yields its sampled version at times $nT_s$, denoted as $\ell_{\delta} (t)$: $$ \ell_{\delta} (t) = \ell(t) \delta_{T_s}(t) = \ell(t) \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t-n T_s) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \ell_s [ n ] \delta(t-n T_s) $$ (see figure: Sampling a signal using the delta train.)
concepts.motivation_md: Modeling sampling as a multiplication with a delta train allows engineers to apply continuous-time Fourier analysis to discrete-time sampling problems.
concepts.recap_md: - Sampling is modeled by multiplying a continuous signal with a periodic delta train.- The resulting sampled signal is a sequence of impulses weighted by the original signal's values.

concepts.title: Sampling in the Fourier Domain
concepts.one_liner: Sampling in the time domain corresponds to the periodic replication of the signal's spectrum in the Fourier domain.
concepts.content: The continuous Fourier transform of the sampled signal $\ell_{\delta} (t)$ is the convolution of the Fourier transforms of $\ell(t)$ and the delta train $\delta_{T_s}(t)$. The Fourier transform of a delta comb is: $$ \Delta_{T_s} (w) = \frac{2\pi}{T_s} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta \left(w-k \frac{2 \pi}{T_s} \right) $$ The result is that the Fourier transform of an impulse train is also an impulse train but with a frequency displacement that grows when the spacing in time decreases: $$ \delta_{T_s}(t) \xrightarrow{\mathscr{F}} \delta_{\frac{2 \pi}{T_s}}(w) $$ [FIGURE:fe58e7c77a4e1cca | Delta train with period $T_s$.] [FIGURE:0522d20216d13776 | Fourier transform of delta train.] Therefore, the continuous Fourier transform of $\ell_{\delta} (t)$ can be written as: $$ \mathscr{L}_{\delta} (w) = \frac{2\pi}{T_s} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \mathscr{L} \left(w-k \frac{2 \pi}{T_s} \right) $$ This equation shows that $\mathscr{L}_{\delta} (w)$ is built as an infinite sum of translated copies of $\mathscr{L}(w)$. If $T_s$ is large, these copies will overlap and produce aliasing. (see figure: Sketch to illustrate aliasing. concepts.recap_md: - Sampling a signal in time creates periodic copies of its spectrum in the frequency domain.- Aliasing occurs when these spectral copies overlap because the sampling rate is too low.

concepts.title: Ideal Reconstruction
concepts.one_liner: Ideal reconstruction recovers a continuous signal from its samples by convolving them with a sinc function, effectively applying a low-pass filter.
concepts.content: When the Nyquist condition is satisfied, it is possible to reconstruct the original continuous signal from the samples using a box filter that has a constant gain for all the frequencies inside $w \in \left[-\pi / T_s, \pi / T_s \right]$, and 0 outside: $$ H(w) = \begin{cases} \frac{T_s}{2\pi} & \text{if } w \in \left[-\pi / T_s, \pi / T_s \right]\\ 0 & \text{otherwise } \end{cases} $$ The impulse response of such a filter is $h(t) = \text{sinc} (t/T_s)$ where $\text{sinc} (t) = \frac{\sin (\pi t)}{\pi t}$. The sinc function is an infinite-length continuous signal that has its maximum at the origin, $\text{sinc} (0)=1$, and is symmetrical. (see figure: Sinc function. This signal is a modulated sine signal with an amplitude decay of $1/t$. The frequency is normalized so that the zero crossings happen at integer values.) Under the slow and smooth prior, this is the optimal reconstruction in terms of the L2 norm. The reconstructed signal $\widetilde \ell(t)$ is: $$ \widetilde \ell(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \ell_s[n] \text{sinc} \left(\frac{t-nT_s}{T_s} \right) $$ (see figure: Smooth interpolation of the sampled function using sinc functions.)
concepts.motivation_md: Ideal reconstruction defines the theoretical limit of how accurately a signal can be recovered from its samples, providing a benchmark for practical interpolation methods.
concepts.recap_md: - Perfect reconstruction is possible by convolving samples with a sinc function if the Nyquist condition is met.- This process is equivalent to applying an ideal low-pass box filter in the frequency domain.

concepts.title: Sinc function
concepts.one_liner: The sinc function is defined as $\text{sinc}(t) = \frac{\sin(\pi t)}{\pi t}$ and serves as the ideal interpolation kernel for band-limited signals.
concepts.content: The sinc function is defined as: $$ \text{sinc} (t) = \frac{\sin (\pi t)}{\pi t} $$ The sinc function is an infinite-length continuous signal that has its maximum at the origin, $\text{sinc} (0)=1$, it is symmetrical, $\text{sinc} (t) = \text{sinc} (-t)$, and it is a sinusoidal wave with a period of 2 that decays in amplitude at a rate $1/t$. (see figure: Sinc function. This signal is a modulated sine signal with an amplitude decay of $1/t$. The frequency is normalized so that the zero crossings happen at integer values.)
concepts.motivation_md: The sinc function is the fundamental building block for perfect reconstruction and low-pass filtering in digital signal processing.
concepts.recap_md: - The sinc function is defined as $\text{sinc}(t) = \sin(\pi t) / (\pi t)$.- It is a symmetrical signal that decays at a rate of $1/t$ and has zero crossings at integer values.

concepts.title: Nearest neighbor interpolation
concepts.one_liner: Nearest neighbor interpolation assigns the value of the closest sample in time to each point in the reconstructed signal.
concepts.content: In 1D, some of the most popular interpolation kernels are nearest interpolation and linear interpolation. Nearest interpolation consists of assigning to each time instant the value of the nearest sample in time, while linear interpolation consists of interpolating linearly between two consecutive values. Both can be modeled as a linear convolution with a kernel $h(t)$. Nearest neighbor interpolation is the result of the convolution of $\ell_\delta (t)$ with a box of width $T_s$, whereas in linear interpolation, the kernel $h(t)$ is a triangle of width $2T_s$. (see figure: (top) Nearest interpolation. (bottom) Linear interpolation. Both interpolation methods can be modeled by a convolution with the kernel shown in the middle (a box and a triangle).)
concepts.motivation_md: While not as accurate as sinc interpolation, nearest neighbor and linear interpolation are widely used in real-time applications due to their computational simplicity.
concepts.recap_md: - Nearest neighbor interpolation uses a box kernel for convolution to assign the value of the closest sample.- Linear interpolation uses a triangular kernel to calculate values by creating a straight line between adjacent samples.

prereq.rationale: Aliasing is a phenomenon that arises specifically during the process of sampling a signal.
The occurrence of aliasing depends on the choice of sampling parameters, such as the period between samples.
Understanding how to exploit aliasing for superresolution requires first understanding what aliasing is as a sampling artifact.
Understanding spatiotemporal sampling requires knowledge of aliasing, specifically temporal aliasing artifacts like the wagon-wheel effect.
Anti-aliasing filters are necessary in spatiotemporal sampling to prevent temporal and spatial artifacts.
Global shutter mode relies on a regular spatial 2D grid for its sampling structure.
The sampling period is a fundamental parameter that defines the temporal or spatial interval of the sampling process.
The analysis of 2D aliasing involves multiplying the image with a delta train to model the sampling process.
Understanding how the 2D Fourier transform changes during subsampling is necessary to explain aliasing artifacts.
The purpose of an anti-aliasing filter is to ensure the signal is band-limited before it is sampled.
Anti-aliasing filters are used to satisfy the conditions of the Sampling Theorem by removing frequencies above the Nyquist limit.
Lanczos-1 interpolation is explicitly defined as using the central lobe of the sinc function as its kernel.
Rectangular sampling is the standard 2D application of the general sampling concept to images.
Hexagonal sampling is an alternative 2D sampling pattern for discrete images.
Irregular sampling is a non-grid-based approach to the general problem of signal sampling.
The 2D sampled signal is modeled mathematically by multiplying the continuous signal with a 2D delta train.
The concept of optimal 2D sampling identifies regular hexagonal sampling as the superior strategy.
Optimality is determined by analyzing spectral replicas in the Fourier domain to maximize resolution without aliasing.
Ideal reconstruction is the inverse process of sampling and is only theoretically possible when the Nyquist condition, defined by the Sampling Theorem, is satisfied.
The sampling theorem's criterion depends on the existence of a maximum frequency present in the signal.
The Nyquist criterion is derived from the requirement that spectral replicas in the Fourier domain do not overlap.
Radian frequency is defined in terms of the period of the signal.
The sampling process is modeled mathematically by multiplying a signal with a delta train.
The frequency domain analysis is based on the time-domain multiplication model of sampling.

overlay.rationale: While anti-aliasing filters aim to remove aliasing to prevent artifacts, superresolution algorithms seek to exploit those same patterns to recover information.
Superresolution aims to recover high-frequency content that is traditionally considered lost according to the limits of the sampling theorem.
Global shutter is the most common form of regular spatiotemporal sampling.
Rolling shutter is a specific spatiotemporal sampling strategy where rows are sampled at different time instants.
Rolling shutter samples rows at different times, whereas global shutter exposes all pixels simultaneously.
Moire patterns are interference phenomena closely related to the concept of aliasing.
Aliasing in 2D images is a specific application of the general aliasing phenomenon to two-dimensional signals.
Anti-aliasing filters are the primary technique used to mitigate the 2D aliasing artifacts described in the previous concept.
Lanczos-1 is presented as an alternative local interpolation method to linear or cubic interpolation.
Hexagonal sampling is contrasted with the more common rectangular grid sampling pattern.
The 2D Fourier transform of a sampled signal generalizes the 1D result of shifted spectral replicas to a 2D grid defined by a sampling matrix.
Linear interpolation is a common practical reconstruction method that approximates the ideal sinc interpolation using a finite-support triangular kernel.
Nearest neighbor and linear interpolation are both popular 1D interpolation techniques that use different kernels to approximate the original signal.
Nearest neighbor interpolation is a simple, non-ideal reconstruction method compared to the theoretically perfect but infinite-support sinc reconstruction.
The sampling theorem provides the theoretical condition to avoid the phenomenon of aliasing.
